title: When something goes wrong
job: Problems, asking for help, complaining calmly
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: quid accidit? IS A PERFECT, AND IT IS ALSO ITS OWN PRESENT. 'What happened?' is a completed event, so the perfect is right — and accidit is one of a handful of Latin verbs whose perfect and present are spelled identically, with no macron to part them. Only the sentence around it decides. L1-M5's review recorded the same thing about bibit; the honest course names it rather than hiding it, because a learner will meet it and be puzzled.

ASKING FOR HELP IS BUILT ENTIRELY FROM WHAT THE LEVEL ALREADY TAUGHT: adiuvā mē, quaesō — an order shape like M5's bibe, M1's mē, M1's quaesō. Or the noun, with no preposition: auxilium rogō, 'I ask help', because rogō takes what you want as a plain object. The third module running where an English preposition has nowhere to attach.

THE THINGS THAT GO WRONG ARE PARTICIPLES TAUGHT AS ADJECTIVES, and that is a decision rather than a simplification. frāctus est looks like a passive and IS one in full Latin; here it is a word that AGREES — frāctus, frācta, frāctum — used with sum, because the passive system is L4-M7's. What you learn is L2-M3's agreement on a new kind of word, and no tense at all. An author who explains the construction has opened the passive two levels early.

nōn inveniō MEANS 'I CANNOT FIND', AND THE GAP IS NAMED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER. This course has no verb for 'can' — possum is taught in neither L1 nor L2 — so 'I do not find' carries the work. Latin does without 'can' far more readily than English, and a learner reaching for possum is reaching for a later level.

LATIN COMPLAINS BY STATING THE FACT, AND THERE IS NOTHING TO SOFTEN IT WITH. errāvī is 'I was wrong' and errāvistī is 'you were wrong', and quaesō — which softens any request — cannot touch either: it means 'I beg' and there is nothing to beg for in a statement. L1-M10's ignōsce ('forgive me') is the nearest thing to an apology the course has. An English speaker will look for a hedge and there is none to find.

words.note: 'What', asking. L1-M2's word, and here it is the subject of the verb rather than the object — 'what happened', not 'what did you do'.
'It happened' — a completed event, so a perfect. The same shape is ALSO its own present, 'it happens', and only context decides which: Latin has a handful of verbs like this.

sentences.trap: accidit is two tenses in one spelling. It is 'it happened' and 'it happens', with nothing to tell them apart but the sentence around it — and L1-M5 met the same thing in bibit. This course writes every macron it can and this pair has no macron to write.

variations.changed: L1-M5's herī, which settles the tense
a name added, which needs no new shape for Iūlia
M1's tibi, which makes it personal

sentences.mnemonic: One spelling, two tenses, and the sentence decides.

words.note: 'Help!' — an order, like M5's bibe and L1-M8's dā. The verb is adiuvō, and asking for help in Latin is a command with quaesō on it.
'Me' — the object shape of L1-M2's tū family: ego 'I', mē 'me'. M1's row, and it is the one pronoun this module needs.
'Please', literally 'I beg'. M1's word. It softens a REQUEST and it cannot soften a complaint — there is nothing in Latin that does.

sentences.trap: Every word here is already yours. The order shape is M5's pattern, mē is M1's row, quaesō is M1's word — so the level's hardest ask is built out of the level's own vocabulary, which is what a module this late should feel like.

variations.changed: quaesō dropped, which is urgent rather than rude
the noun and a plain statement instead of an order
M6's nōs as the object, which does not change shape

sentences.usage: Said when you need someone now.

words.note: 'Help', the thing rather than the act — and it is neuter, so it does not change between subject and object. English 'auxiliary' is the same word.
'I ask, I ask for': rogō 'I ask', rogat 'he asks'. It takes the thing asked for as a plain object, with no preposition — no Latin 'for'.

sentences.trap: No 'for'. rogō takes what you are asking for as its object directly, so auxilium rogō is 'I ask help' — and adding a preposition would be the same mistake as putting one in front of raedā or hōrā, three modules running.

variations.cue: I am asking for help, please.
I am not asking for help.

sentences.usage: Said when you would rather state it than demand it.

words.note: 'Telephone' — M7's modern word, and it is neuter, so it looks the same as a subject and as an object.
'Broken' — an adjective here, not a tense, so it agrees: frāctus, frācta, frāctum. This is the neuter, matching tēlephōnum.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: frāctum est looks like one thing and is being taught as another. In full Latin it is a passive — 'it was broken' — and this course teaches it as an adjective with 'is', because the whole passive system belongs to L4-M7. What you learn here is a word that agrees, not a tense.

variations.changed: a feminine thing, so the adjective moves

mistake.why: the masculine ending on a neuter noun, because frāctus is the shape you meet first. It is L2-M3's error arriving on a new kind of word — and it is the reason this module teaches the participle as an adjective, because an adjective is a thing you already know how to make agree.

sentences.usage: Said about something that has stopped working.
sentences.mnemonic: It agrees, so it is an adjective.

words.note: 'Book' as the object: liber as the subject, librum as the thing looked for. L1-M4's word.
'Not', in front of what it denies. L1-M3's word.
'I find' — built on L1-M9's veniō, which is why it looks familiar: 'come upon'. inveniō 'I find', invenit 'he finds'.

sentences.trap: This says 'I do not find' and means 'I cannot find'. This course has no verb for 'can' — possum is not taught in L1 or L2 — so the gap is named rather than papered over: a learner reaching for 'cannot' is reaching for a later level, and Latin manages without it more often than English does.

words.note: 'I went wrong, I made a mistake' — a plain perfect of errō, and L1-M5's -vī ending unchanged. English 'error' and 'erratic' are the same word.

sentences.trap: One word, and no softening anywhere. Latin complains and admits fault by stating the fact — quaesō softens a request and nothing softens a statement, so an English speaker looking for 'I'm afraid I may have…' will find there is nothing to build it out of.
sentences.sound: er-RĀ-vī. Two long vowels at the end, and the stress on the first of them: L1-M5's perfect ending, audible.

variations.changed: L1-M10's ignōsce, which is as close to an apology as Latin gets

sentences.usage: Said when you admit a mistake.

sentences.cue: I was not wrong; YOU were wrong.

words.note: 'Not', in front of what it denies.
'I went wrong' — the perfect of errō, L1-M5's ending.
'You', one person. L1-M2's row, and it is here for stress: errāvistī already says who, so the pronoun is the accusation.
'You went wrong' — the perfect's you-shape, which is -istī where the present is -ās. L1-M5 wrote the I and he shapes; this is the third.

sentences.trap: tū is doing the whole work of the quarrel. The ending already says who, so writing the pronoun is what makes it pointed — and that is the same fact L1-M10 and M6 both spent a rule on, arriving in the one place where being pointed is the purpose.

variations.cue: I was not wrong; Marcus was wrong.
variations.changed: a name instead of an accusation
the bare charge, with no denial in front of it

sentences.mnemonic: The pronoun is the pointed finger.

sentences.cue: The table is broken; what happened?

words.note: 'Table' — mēnsa as the subject, mēnsam as the object. L1-M3's word.
'Broken' — and it is being taught as an ADJECTIVE, so it agrees: frāctus for a masculine thing, frācta for a feminine one. English 'fracture' is the same word.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.
'What', asking, and the subject of the verb after it.
'It happened' — the perfect, and also its own present. Here the broken table settles it: something already happened.

sentences.trap: Here the context does the work the macron cannot. accidit is 'it happens' and 'it happened' both, and a table that is already broken can only mean the past — which is what 'only context decides' looks like when you are actually reading.

variations.cue: The book is broken; what happened?
The table is broken; I was wrong.
The telephone is broken; what happened?

sentences.cue: Help me: I cannot find the book.

words.note: 'Help!' — the order shape of adiuvō, softened by quaesō when you want it and not otherwise.
'Me' — the object shape of L1-M2's tū family: ego 'I', mē 'me'. M1's row, and it is the one pronoun this module needs.
'Book' as the thing looked for.
'Not', in front of what it denies.
'I find', built on veniō — and with nōn it is how this course says 'I cannot find'.

sentences.trap: The order and the reason, with nothing between them but a pause. Latin does not need 'because' here — L1-M9's quia and quod exist and are not required — and the whole request is built from words the level has already taught.

variations.display: Adiuvā mē, quaesō: librum nōn inveniō.
variations.cue: Help me, please: I cannot find the book.
Help me: I cannot find the telephone.

variations.display: Adiuvā mē, quia librum nōn inveniō.
variations.cue: Help me, because I cannot find the book.
variations.changed: L1-M9's quia making the reason explicit

sentences.usage: Said when you have given up looking.

sentences.cue: I was wrong: I did not leave a message.

words.note: 'I went wrong' — the perfect of errō.
'Message' — nūntius as the subject, nūntium as the thing left. M7's word.
'Not', in front of what it denies.
'I left behind' — the perfect of M7's relinquō, and it drops the n and lengthens the i: relinquō, relīquī. L1-M5 said the perfect often rebuilds the word rather than adding to it.

sentences.trap: relīquī is relinquō with its middle taken out. The perfect in Latin is not a suffix on the present — L1-M5 established that with vēnī from veniō — and this is the same fact on a verb you met three modules ago, which is where it starts to cost you.
sentences.sound: er-RĀ-vī: NŪN-ti-um nōn re-LĪ-quī. Five long vowels, and the two perfects both end on one.

variations.cue: I was wrong: I DID leave a message.
variations.changed: the negative dropped, so the mistake was the opposite one

variations.cue: I was wrong: I cannot find the telephone.
variations.changed: a present reason for a past mistake

variations.cue: I did not leave a message; I shall telephone again.

mistake.why: the perfect built by adding to the present, which is how a learner expects it to work after errō gave errāvī. relinquō does not do that, and neither does veniō, habeō or legō — the -vī perfect is the regular one and it is not the common one.

sentences.usage: Said owning up to something you forgot.

comprehensionPool.cue: I did not leave a message.
The book is broken; what happened?
